The Rain That Was Killing Lakes: How Cap-and-Trade Fixed Acid Rain

In the 1970s, rain was killing lakes across the United States. Scientists spent 18 years trying to prove it. The fix came from an unlikely source: a market mechanism that worked better than anyone predicted.

The Lake That Had No Fish

In 1972, Gene Likens stood at the edge of a stream in the White Mountains of New Hampshire. He had been measuring the water chemistry at Hubbard Brook since 1963. For years, he noticed something strange. The rain falling on the forest was acidic. Not a little. A pH of 4.03. That is 30 times more acidic than normal rain.

Likens was a limnologist, a scientist who studies lakes and streams. He knew what that number meant. Acid kills aquatic life. It leaches aluminum from soil into streams. It destroys the food chain. And it was not just Hubbard Brook. Rain all across the northeastern US was becoming acid.

Likens published his findings in 1974. The reaction from industry was immediate. Utilities argued the problem was natural. President Reagan later joked that "trees cause pollution." The government set up studies to delay action. For 18 years, the scientists who discovered acid rain watched their country do nothing while lakes died.

This is the story of how they finally fixed it. Not through idealism, but through a market.

The 18-Year Delay

By 1980, the evidence was overwhelming. Hundreds of lakes in the Adirondacks were dead. Fish gone. Water clear and empty. Forests on mountain tops were losing their leaves. Statues and buildings were dissolving. The rain falling on the eastern US was as acidic as lemon juice.

The cause was clear. Coal-burning power plants in the Midwest were sending sulfur dioxide into the air. The wind carried it hundreds of miles east. It mixed with water vapor and fell as sulfuric acid on New England, New York, and Canada.

Congress passed the Acid Deposition Act in 1980. It funded research. It did not regulate anything. The National Academy of Sciences urged action. President Reagan dismissed the problem. Political gridlock set in. The problem was real, the science was clear, and the solution was blocked by the very industries causing it.

The low point came in the mid-1980s. Lake acidity was still rising. Forests were still dying. Likens had been collecting data for 15 years, watching his predictions come true, unable to make Washington act.

Then a new president, George H.W. Bush, made a different bet. He decided to solve acid rain with a market.

The Cap-and-Trade Invention

The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments created the Acid Rain Program. It was a radical experiment. Instead of telling every power plant how much to cut, the government set a hard cap on total emissions. Then it issued tradable allowances. Each allowance let a plant emit one ton of sulfur dioxide. If a plant cut its emissions below its allowance, it could sell the extra allowance to another plant. If a plant could not cut cheaply, it could buy allowances from someone who already did.

The total cap was 8.95 million tons per year, down from 18.9 million in 1980. A 50% reduction. The system was phased in: Phase I in 1995 covered the 261 dirtiest generating units. Phase II in 2000 covered all plants over 75 megawatts.

This was the first large-scale experiment with market-based environmental regulation. Economists loved the theory. Environmentalists were skeptical. Would it really work to let polluters buy and sell the right to pollute?

The answer surprised everyone.

It Worked Faster Than Anyone Predicted

The Acid Rain Program exceeded its targets within years. SO2 emissions dropped 43% from 1990 levels by 2000. That was faster than required. The cost was a fraction of what industry predicted. The original estimate was $2-4 billion per year. The actual cost was around $1 billion. The market found the cheapest cuts first. Plants that could add scrubbers cheaply did so. Others bought allowances from cleaner plants. The invisible hand solved a problem that regulation could not.

A 2021 study found the program reduced mortality risk by 5% over 10 years. Fewer heart attacks. Fewer asthma cases. Cleaner air.

The lakes are recovering. Slowly. The Adirondacks have started to see fish return. pH levels are rising. The forests are showing signs of recovery. It takes decades for an ecosystem to heal, but the damage has stopped getting worse.

"The Acid Rain Program demonstrated that market-based approaches can achieve environmental goals faster and cheaper than traditional regulation. It is one of the most successful environmental programs in US history."
- Environmental Protection Agency

There is unfinished business. Agricultural runoff continues to acidify some waters. The program was weakened by later court decisions. But the core story holds: a problem that seemed unsolvable in 1980, blocked by industry and politics, was solved by a surprisingly simple market mechanism.

The Lakes You Never Knew Were Dying

Here is the part that matters. You have never thought about acid rain. You have never worried that the lake you swim in might be dead. You have never checked the pH of the rain falling on your roof. In the 1990s, acid rain was a front-page story. Children learned about it in school. Environmental groups held protests. Now, it is a solved problem that nobody mentions.

The rain is still acidic in some places, but not dangerously so. The lakes are coming back. The forests are recovering. And they recovered because a group of scientists refused to stop collecting data for 18 years, a president decided to try something new, and a market mechanism ended up being cheaper than anyone thought possible.

The lesson of acid rain is not that markets always work. It is that when the problem is clear, when the science is settled, and when the political will finally exists, we have more tools than we think. Cap-and-trade was an experiment. It succeeded beyond expectations. And the lakes that were silent for decades are now, slowly, filling with life again.

Next time you stand at the edge of a lake in the Adirondacks, ask yourself: is this lake alive? If it is, someone like Gene Likens is part of the reason why.
